sentences.t: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement launched drone strikes that hit near Saudi Arabia's Shaybah oilfield - one of the kingdom's largest - and attacked Dammam's civilian airport on Wednesday, killing two people there and two more at a Saudi oilfield, the Guardian reported.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said four vessels were hit or caught fire in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel for roughly a fifth of the world's oil.
Brent crude settled up 4% at $113.17 a barrel, its highest close since early May, and US WTI settled up 2.4% at $99.47 (WSJ; the Guardian had reported Brent near $112 during trading).

The diplomacy is moving in two directions at once, and both accounts are on the record: CBS News reports the US is reducing its Middle East troop footprint as indirect talks with Iran continue, while President Trump denied any talks the same day and hinted at further strikes - "We've knocked the hell out of them, and we may do it a little bit further" (Al Jazeera's live coverage).
The IRGC, for its part, threatened to extend confrontation to US bases.
That is a named conflict between the two accounts, and it is unresolved.

Why it matters to you: crude is the single input that connects your world this month - imported inflation, the RBI's "calibrated tightening" stance, the 10-year at 7.46%, and every insurer's bond book.
A supply scare that holds $112 into next week's Fed decision hardens the higher-for-longer story on both sides of the world.
Editor's takeaway: oil markets are now pricing actual damage near Saudi infrastructure, not the threat of it - the five-month high is the receipt.
The S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, or 1.2%, to 7,663.43 on Thursday - its worst day since July - and the Nasdaq dropped 694 points, or 2.6%, to 26,008.86, its worst since June (AP's post-close wrap).
The Dow rose 11.89 points to 52,867.98 and the Russell 2000 edged up 0.1% to 2,784.03; most US stocks actually rose, which tells you the damage was concentrated in the AI megacaps.
Meta fell about 7% despite beating revenue expectations and guiding higher: CNBC's read of the results is that AI spending pushed free cash flow negative.
Chips fell with it - AMD and Intel about 8%, Micron 6%, Nvidia 4%, CoreWeave 10% - even as Jensen Huang told CNBC that demand from the new cloud providers is "off the charts".
The counterweights were old economy: Procter & Gamble rose more than 5% and Blackstone jumped on their own results (CNBC; Yahoo Finance).
Treasury yields fell on the risk move, the 10-year to about 4.97% (CNBC), and weekly jobless claims came in at 194,000 against a 200,000 survey (Labor Department data).

Why it matters to you: this is the first session where the market punished the AI build-out's cost rather than rewarding its promise - and India's IT complex, your watchlist's core, takes its cue from exactly this trade.
Infosys reports today into that tape.
Editor's takeaway: the question shifted overnight from "who is spending most on AI" to "who can show what it earns" - and the first answer the market got was negative cash flow.

The Sensex fell 460.30 points (0.62%) to 73,249.39 and the Nifty 123.70 (0.54%) to 22,687.65 on Thursday - a third consecutive fall, about 2% over the three sessions, leaving the index 14% below its 52-week high and 2.3% above its low (Business Standard).
The Nifty recovered from a 22,554.85 intraday low to close near 22,688 after testing 22,785 mid-recovery.
Bank Nifty fell only 0.09% to 54,925.70, outperforming the index for once, with Bajaj Finance, ICICI Bank and SBI among the Nifty's top gainers.
The rupee snapped an eight-session winning streak, falling 36 paise to 94.82 per dollar as crude topped $112 (The Hindu BusinessLine).
The 10-year government bond yield closed at 7.46% (ET Markets data; countryeconomy's daily table corroborates 7.46% for 22 October), up about 69 basis points in ten weeks.
Foreign investors net sold ₹3,459 crore while domestic institutions bought ₹2,891 crore (moneycontrol's exchange-data wrap).
Breadth was ugly: declines outnumbered advances by more than two to one on every count (moneycontrol; ET's NSE tally), and the midcap and smallcap indices fell harder than the large caps.

Why it matters to you: three straight oil-driven falls with a weakening rupee is the exact configuration that tests the RBI's stance - and it reprices everything you track, from NBFC funding costs to insurer treasury books.
Watch whether banks keep absorbing the shock better than the index; that is where the rate story shows up first.

Editor's takeaway: the index fell less than the world around it, and banks finally outperformed - domestic buyers are still absorbing foreign selling, but the rupee and the bond yield are now moving against them at the same time.
India's largest-ever IPO - Jio Platforms' ₹30,213 crore all-fresh issue at ₹1,065-1,119 - ends today: bidding closes at 5 PM and UPI mandates at 7 PM.

The settled day-two print, on BSE consolidated bid data as of 7 PM Thursday (NDTV Profit's timestamped live-blog final, matching Mint's table): overall 5.57 times, institutions (QIBs) 13.29 times, non-institutional bidders 5.97 times, retail 1.54 times, Reliance shareholders 4.05 times, employees 2.10 times.
NSE's consolidated schedule showed 5.36 times with QIBs at 12.87 times excluding anchor allotments - a different exchange cut and anchor treatment of the same demand.
The anchor book of about ₹8,110 crore was placed on 19 October.
Allotment is expected Monday 26 October and listing Wednesday 28 October on BSE and NSE.
At the ₹1,119 cap the company is valued at about ₹10.3 lakh crore (~$108 billion), which would make it India's fourth-most-valuable listed company on debut (Fortune India; Times of India).
Grey-market premium - unofficial - was last at ₹246, about 22% over the cap (investorgain, 22 Oct morning).
Why it matters to you: retail crossed full subscription only on day two and sits at 1.54 times - allotment in this issue is a lottery, not a given, and today's final print decides the odds.
The listing also redraws India's market-cap map: the RIL group would pass the Tata group in combined value.

Editor's takeaway: the demand question is answered; what Wednesday's open prices is whether ₹10.3 lakh crore is a floor or a ceiling for a business whose growth now comes from tariff hikes, not subscriber additions.
Swiggy's board approved September-quarter results between 3:00 and 3:40 PM Thursday (exchange intimation).
On the company's shareholder-letter basis, consolidated Adjusted Revenue rose 33.8% on the year to ₹7,909 crore and the consolidated Adjusted EBITDA loss was ₹760 crore.
Food delivery is now reliably profitable: gross order value up 17.7% to ₹10,054 crore with Adjusted EBITDA of ₹341 crore - a record 3.4% margin.
Quick commerce (Instamart) is where the money goes: order value up 31.4% to ₹9,230 crore across 1,240 dark stores in 133 cities, with an Adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹895 crore, a 9.7% negative margin.

On the exchange-filing basis NDTV Profit tracked, net loss narrowed to ₹922 crore from ₹1,092 crore a year ago but came in wider than the ₹871 crore analysts estimated; reported revenue rose 36.1% to ₹7,571 crore - a different, narrower revenue definition than the letter's Adjusted Revenue, so the two bases should not be mixed.

The structural news: shareholders approved capping foreign ownership at 49.5%, making Swiggy "Indian Owned and Controlled", which lets Instamart own its inventory outright - a shift the company estimates is worth about 80 basis points of contribution margin once fully implemented, with the transition starting mid-Q3 and running two to three quarters (ET, 22 Oct).

Why it matters to you: this is the cleanest public dataset on Indian quick-commerce unit economics - the exact trade-off (record margins in the mature engine funding the burn in the growth engine) that every consumer-internet product team, yours included, has to sequence.
The IOC restructuring is also a template: ownership structure as a margin lever.

Editor's takeaway: the street wanted the burn to shrink with scale; instead it grew ₹118 crore quarter on quarter while food delivery printed a record - the question is no longer whether the model works, but how long investors fund the second engine.
Thursday's session never gave the bulls a window.

The Nifty opened weak with global markets, fell to 22,554.85 by early afternoon, and even a recovery attempt stalled below 22,785 before the close at 22,687.65 - the index has now given up about 2% in three sessions and sits closer to its 52-week low (+2.3%) than its high (-14%).

The selling was broadest where it hurts most: the smallcap index's 1.14% fall took it to its lowest since 12 June, and declines outnumbered advances by more than two to one on the day (moneycontrol; Business Standard; ET's NSE tally).
Under the surface, the leverage is coming off.

Margin-trading books shrank to ₹1.56 lakh crore from September's ₹1.6 lakh crore record - the first monthly decline since March - and global funds have pulled more than $32 billion from Indian equities this year, a record, with the NSE 500 down 9% from its September peak (The Hindu BusinessLine).
The overnight tape offers no relief: Asia followed Wall Street down on Friday morning, with Seoul's KOSPI opening 2.36% lower on the AI selloff and oil (Yonhap, 9:03 AM Seoul time).

The configuration to watch: crude at a five-month high, the rupee weakening, the 10-year rising and foreign investors selling - all four pressures pointing the same way for the first time in this move, while domestic institutions keep absorbing the supply.
Gainers, large cap: Bajaj Finance +1.74% (₹942.10) - recovering part of Wednesday's 3.3% margin-warning slide; no fresh company news.
Cipla +1.29% and Sun Pharma +0.74% - pharma led defensives on a risk-off day.
UltraTech Cement +1.00% - extending its post-results move (September-quarter profit ₹1,501 crore, up 21.3%).
ICICI Bank +0.97%, SBI +0.73%, Axis Bank +0.17% - lenders were the session's pocket of strength; Federal Bank (+1.10%) led the Bank Nifty.
(Closing data: AlphaTribe's NSE snapshot, 4 PM.)
Results boards: today - Infosys, Dr Reddy's Laboratories, IndusInd Bank, JSW Steel, Adani Power, BPCL, Coforge, Tata Motors PV, CG Power.
Saturday - Kotak Mahindra Bank, IDFC First Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Castrol India (The Hindu BusinessLine; TotalMarket results calendar).

Hindustan Petroleum posted a standalone profit of ₹3,483 crore for the September quarter - a swing from the ₹11,526 crore loss in the June quarter and far better than the ₹2,050 crore loss analysts had estimated (NDTV Profit's poll).

The year-on-year basis tells the harder story: profit fell 9% from ₹3,830 crore a year ago, because Brent averaged about 40% higher this quarter through the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, squeezing marketing margins - Elara Securities estimates diesel marketing margins were minus ₹24 a litre against plus ₹5 a year ago - and the tax charge more than doubled.
Product sales value rose 26.2% to ₹1.39 lakh crore (Business Standard).
Both bases matter: a big beat against expectations, a decline against last year.

Colgate-Palmolive India's profit rose 4.3% to ₹342 crore on revenue up 12.2% at ₹1,706 crore, but missed estimates (₹368 crore profit, 29.9% margin expected; 27.8% delivered) in its first quarter under a new CEO; toothpaste volumes grew in the high single digits (Business Standard).
Havells' profit rose 11.4% to ₹353 crore on revenue up 34.6%.
Cyient's profit rose 16.6% sequentially to ₹121 crore with EBIT margin up at 10.21%.
CreditAccess Grameen - India's largest microfinance lender - earned ₹502 crore against ₹129 crore a year ago and raised FY27 return-on-assets guidance to 5.2-5.8%.
Adani Energy Solutions' profit jumped to ₹1,323 crore from ₹534 crore on revenue up 52.8%; Adani Total Gas earned ₹173 crore, up 22.3% sequentially.

Elsewhere: Jindal Stainless ₹895 crore (+16.4% QoQ), Chennai Petroleum ₹2,271 crore (more than double QoQ), Nippon Life India AMC ₹324 crore (-35.7% QoQ on a one-time ₹97 crore loss), J&K Bank ₹546 crore (+10.5% YoY), and BlueStone narrowed its loss to ₹4.4 crore while planning a ₹300 crore bond raise.

SEBI has proposed that market infrastructure institutions - the exchanges and depositories that sit at the centre of Indian markets - be allowed to invest in businesses related to their core functions without prior SEBI approval.

The waiver would cover investments mandated by SEBI itself, subsidiary investments from internal funds, and entities regulated by other financial regulators, with board oversight and safeguards substituted for case-by-case permission.
Public comments are open until 12 November (Reuters).

The mechanism matters: BSE Ltd, CDSL and their peers currently need the regulator's sign-off for adjacent bets; the proposal converts permission into governance, which is how an exchange becomes a broader financial-infrastructure company.

Why it matters to you: BSE and CDSL are watchlist staples whose optionality has been capped by exactly this approval rule; and for anyone building in fintech or insurance distribution, the regulator's posture here - governance over gatekeeping - is the same posture showing up in the IRDAI distribution paper.

A SEBI circular dated 22 October waives margin on subsequent buy or sell transactions once a client has made an early pay-in (EPI) - delivering shares or funds to the broker before settlement - with the EPI value now calculated on the trade day.
In plain terms: a client who delivers early no longer has margin blocked twice on the same capital.
The relief is mechanical, not headline-grabbing, but margin blocked is the binding constraint on how much a broker's clients can trade - this frees it.

Margin-trading positions - money borrowed from brokers to buy shares - fell to ₹1.56 lakh crore from September's ₹1.6 lakh crore record, the first monthly decline since March (The Hindu BusinessLine).
It pairs with the flow data: global funds have pulled a record $32 billion-plus from Indian equities in 2026, and the NSE 500 sits 9% below its September peak.
Deleveraging after a record is how corrections usually end - slowly, and with weaker hands gone first.

Why it matters to you: falling leverage is the precondition for a durable bottom, not the bottom itself; it tells you the froth is leaving smallcaps - where your watchlist's risk lives - before it leaves the index.
Swiggy's structural play is the quarter's real news.

Buried under the earnings miss is an approved manoeuvre, not a completed one: shareholders have voted to cap foreign ownership at 49.5%, the "Indian Owned and Controlled" classification Instamart needs before it can own its inventory instead of operating as a marketplace - the transition itself starts mid-Q3 and runs two to three quarters.
Swiggy estimates the switch is worth about 80 basis points of contribution margin once fully implemented (shareholder letter; ET, 22 Oct).
The aspiration behind it, stated at its first Capital Markets Day on 6 August 2026: ₹10,000 crore of Adjusted EBITDA by FY31 on ₹2.5 lakh crore of gross order value - about a 4% margin.
The build-out is already branded: about 400 brands under its Switch private-label umbrella, and its No!ce value range showing up in one in eight baskets.
The insight: ownership structure is now a P&L decision in Indian consumer internet.

Swiggy is trading shareholder composition for the legal right to hold inventory - because 80 basis points of margin on ₹9,230 crore of quarterly order value is worth more than the strategic flexibility foreign capital above 49.5% would have bought.
Watch whether other inventory-curious platforms run the same play.

Opportunity signal: BlueStone - the online-first jewellery brand that listed this year - narrowed its quarterly loss to ₹4.4 crore and is raising ₹300 crore through non-convertible debentures (NDTV Profit).
Venture debt at near-profitability is the new dilution-avoidance playbook for listed consumer startups; expect more of it as equity stays expensive.
One startup idea: a claims-substantiation service for food and consumer brands.

FSSAI's notices this week to Nestle India and Zydus Wellness (over "easy to digest" and immunity claims on Lactogen, Nan Excella Pro and Complan) plus the regulator's proposal to ban added sucrose and fructose in infant foods up to six months show the enforcement direction: every label claim now needs a scientific file behind it (The Hindu).
A tool that scans a brand's pack copy and ad library against FSSAI's regulations and flags unsubstantiated claims - sold as a subscription audit to D2C food brands - sits exactly on that pain.
First step: parse the FSSAI Act's claims schedule into a machine-checkable rulebook and test it on twenty listed products.
Thursday was the AI trade's first reckoning session.
Meta's record quarter - and its narrowed $135-145 billion capex plan - was read through one line: free cash flow turned negative as AI spending outran it (CNBC).
The stock fell about 7%, and the selloff ran down the supply chain: AMD and Intel about 8%, Micron 6%, Nvidia 4%, CoreWeave 10%.

The bull case was heard too - Nvidia's Jensen Huang told CNBC demand from the new cloud providers is "off the charts" and capital is the scarce resource - and it is worth noting the broader market did not break: most US stocks rose.

Meta separately detailed its plan to issue a new class of non-voting shares as a stock dividend - one Class C share for each Class A and B share, contingent on an amended charter taking effect 19 January 2027, with a two-for-one-split-like effect on the Class A price and no change to voting power (Meta's own release) - a way to keep funding the build-out without diluting control.
Why it matters to you: the AI capex question now has a market-enforced answer format: show the cash.
That reprices the whole chain your work touches - Indian IT services, the model vendors whose APIs you build on, and every startup whose burn is justified by an AI story.
Radar, last 24-48 hours: Anthropic opened a waitlist for Claude Duet, a proactive assistant agent (details in New AI tools, below).

Inception Labs shipped Mercury 3, a diffusion-based text model claiming frontier-class quality at 1,068 tokens per second - vendor-reported, not independently tested; what would count as verification: third-party benchmark runs (below).
TwinMind brought its meeting-memory app to the desktop (below).
OpenAI's models on Google Cloud, announced 21 October, remain in limited preview with general availability "in the coming weeks" (OpenAI) - no GA yet as of this edition.
Nothing else verified in the window worth your attention.

Anthropic announced Claude Duet on 21 October: a research preview of a proactive agent that builds a morning brief from your connected apps, keeps working while you are away, and checks with you before consequential actions.
It runs on Claude Opus 5.5, lives in a standalone iOS/Android app and on claude.ai, and uses a "Managed Agents" design so the agent never sees your passwords, with a classifier gating auto-approvals.
Access: waitlist only, US Pro and Max subscribers first - India availability is not stated, so expect a wait.

Utility for you: the morning-brief pattern is exactly the one this paper runs; Duet is the first mainstream agent packaging it as a product, and the check-before-consequential-actions design is the template to copy in your own agent builds.

Inception Labs released Mercury 3 on 18 October: a diffusion-based large language model the vendor says outperforms GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 while generating at 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs - vendor-reported benchmarks, not independently tested.
Context window is now 1 million tokens (from 260K in Mercury 2.5).
Pricing: $0.20 per million input tokens and $0.70 per million output, with a launch discount of 50% ($0.10/$0.35) and 90% off cached input.
It speaks the OpenAI API format and is available on Inception's platform, OpenRouter, Baseten and Vercel.
Utility for you: at launch pricing it is among the cheapest ways to prototype long-context features - a drop-in base-URL swap lets you A/B it against your current model in an afternoon.

TwinMind - the ambient meeting-memory app - launched its third Product Hunt release this week: a native Mac and Windows app that auto-detects Zoom, Meet and Teams calls and captures transcripts and summaries in 140-plus languages, with a floating mic that dictates cleaned-up text into any app.
Pricing verified at the vendor: the free plan includes unlimited capture hours, summaries and daily digests; Pro is $11.99 a month.
Utility for you: a call-heavy APM week with no bot joining the meeting and no note-taking - the summary lands after.
Caveat: it records from your machine's audio, so tell your call participants it is running.

Mercury 3 is the build-relevant launch this week because of what diffusion generation implies for app architecture: 1,068 tokens per second (vendor-reported) is fast enough to feel instant on long outputs, and at launch pricing a million-token-context call costs cents.

The practical test for your stack: point one non-critical feature - a long summarisation or extraction job - at Mercury 3's OpenAI-compatible endpoint behind a flag, log latency and output quality against your current model for a week, and keep whichever wins on cost-adjusted quality.
Treat the vendor's benchmark table as marketing until third-party runs exist; the price and the API compatibility are the verified, usable facts today.
Automate your meeting notes for one day (about 15 minutes of setup).

Install TwinMind's new desktop app (free plan, linked above), grant microphone and system-audio access, and let it run through your next three calls - it detects Zoom, Meet and Teams automatically, no bot joins.
After the last call, read its summaries and action-item lists against what you would have written.
A good result: three usable summaries with correct names and decisions, and zero minutes spent typing.
Tell participants you are capturing - it records from your machine.
If the summaries hold up, the automation earns its place; if names and numbers drift, you have your answer for free.

In 1998 a young Berkeley economist named Terrance Odean got his hands on something researchers had wanted for decades: the actual trading records of 10,000 individual accounts at a large US discount brokerage, from 1987 to 1993.
Not surveys - trades.
What he found in them has been replicated in market after market since: people sell their winners much more readily than their losers.
Odean counted every position that showed a gain or a loss each day and asked how often each was sold.

Investors realized 14.8% of their available gains but only 9.8% of their available losses ("Are Investors Reluctant to Realize Their Losses?", Journal of Finance, 1998 - the winners they chose to sell went on to beat the losers they kept).
The pattern had been named in 1985 by Hersh Shefrin and Meir Statman: the disposition effect.
One detail redeems us slightly: every December the pattern flips - losses get realized at 12.8% against gains at 10.8% - because a tax bill makes the loss suddenly useful.
The mechanism is not stupidity; it is reference dependence.
A position bought at ₹1,000 is measured against ₹1,000 forever: selling at ₹800 converts "might recover" into "definitely lost", and losing hurts roughly twice what winning feels good.
So the loser is carried - Reliance shareholders holding through an 18% one-year slide into a 52-week low are living the dataset this week - and the winner is banked early to lock the feeling.
The applications reach past trading.

In insurance, the lapse patterns of underperforming endowment and ULIP policies show the same shape: policyholders keep paying into a visibly poor policy because surrendering makes the loss real - persistency teams quietly rely on it.
In product work, users keep paying for subscriptions they no longer use, because cancelling admits the spend was wasted.
In your own portfolio review, the test Odean's data suggests is brutal and simple: would I buy this position fresh today?
The decision rule: write the exit condition when you enter, while the reference price has no grip on you - then review losers as fresh buy decisions, not as recoveries to wait for.
Sixty-second recall: close the page and answer: (1) What is the disposition effect?
(2) Odean's two numbers for gains and losses realized?
(3) Why does December flip the pattern?
(4) The decision rule, in one sentence.
Answers: (1) the tendency to sell winners too early and hold losers too long.
(2) 14.8% of gains realized against 9.8% of losses.
(3) tax-loss selling makes losses useful at year-end.
(4) set exit conditions at entry and judge losers as if deciding fresh.
Delivering your shares (for a sale) or funds (for a purchase) to your broker before the exchange's settlement deadline instead of on settlement day.

When a client pays in early, the obligation is pre-funded - which is why SEBI's circular this week says margin should not also be blocked on the trades that follow: the risk the margin was covering is already gone.
For the client, it means the same capital can support more trading; for the broker, less operational chasing on settlement day.
What I think the market is missing - an analytical read, not advice.

Three sessions in, India's fall is being filed as "global risk-off", but the domestic legs have their own logic: the 10-year at 7.46% is the highest this move has taken it, the rupee's eight-day rise just broke, and Motilal Oswal now expects the repo rate to reach 6.25% this cycle (The Hindu BusinessLine).
I think the tape is starting to price a rate path, not just an oil scare - which is why banks outperformed on a down day: lenders earn the yield curve that hurts everyone else.

My falsifiable marker: if this reading is right, financials keep their relative strength through today's results (IndusInd reports) and the four IPO listings trade weak regardless of their subscription multiples, because liquidity is leaving.
Wrong if the Nifty reclaims 22,900 today on results strength with Brent still above $110, or if Zetwerk opens more than 10% above its cap and holds.
Scoreboard on yesterday's marker: it took its first hit.

I said Bank Nifty would keep underperforming while the 10-year held above about 7.4% - the yield leg held (7.44% to 7.46%) but banks outperformed on Thursday (-0.09% against the Nifty's -0.54%), with Bajaj Finance the Nifty's top gainer.
One day does not kill the marker, but the honest count is: yield leg intact, bank leg broken on day one.

Jio closes today: watch the final print against the settled day-two figure of 5.57 times - a strong close sets up Wednesday's listing to test the ₹10.3 lakh crore valuation; a fade below day-two levels means late bids were pulled.
Wrong if UPI mandate failures distort the final number, which the exchange data will show only on Monday.

IRDAI comments close Sunday 25 October: the distribution-economics paper - expense caps, payout structures - is the biggest live repricing of insurance distribution economics; watch for industry submissions going public over the weekend.
Wrong if the regulator extends the window.

The Fed decides Wednesday 28 October (meeting 27-28, per the Federal Reserve's own calendar), with the ECB and Bank of Japan in the same week: three central banks meeting into an oil spike is a recipe for a rates-led move in everything.
Wrong if Brent gives back the week's gain before Wednesday and takes the urgency with it.

Today, Fri 23 Oct: Jio IPO closes (5 PM bids, 7 PM UPI); Zetwerk, Tonbo Imaging, Bonfiglioli and Sahajanand Medical Technologies list; results from Infosys, Dr Reddy's, IndusInd Bank, JSW Steel, Adani Power, BPCL, Coforge, Tata Motors PV, CG Power; eight dividend ex-dates (above).
US flash PMI tonight, 7:15 PM IST (S&P Global).
Sat 24 Oct: results from Kotak Mahindra Bank, IDFC First Bank, AU Small Finance Bank, Castrol India.
Sun 25 Oct: public comments close on IRDAI's distribution-economics consultation paper.
Mon 26 Oct: Jio Platforms IPO allotment expected.
Tue 27 Oct: L&T Technology Services ₹20 dividend goes ex; the Fed meeting begins in Washington.
Wed 28 Oct: Jio Platforms lists on BSE and NSE; Fed decision; Nippon Life India AMC dividend record date.
X was not accessed for this edition; the launch radar was verified at vendor pages (claude.com, inceptionlabs.ai, twinmind.com) and Product Hunt, with vendor benchmark claims labelled and dated.

A Reuters intraday syndication mislabelled as Thursday's US closing figures (Dow -106.39, S&P 7,647.74, Nasdaq 25,988.10) was caught and rejected; all US closing levels above come from AP's post-close wrap.

New sources in use this edition: NDTV Profit's BSE-attributed IPO live blog (timestamped subscription prints), countryeconomy's daily bond table (10-year corroboration), Yonhap (Seoul open), MarketScreener carrying Reuters (SEBI proposal), claude.com, inceptionlabs.ai, twinmind.com and the Journal of Finance via Wiley (primary paper for the concept).
IPO trackers (ipoguru, ipowatch, mywealthpost) were used as pointers only.
Swiggy figures carry two labelled bases: the company letter's Adjusted Revenue and the exchange-filing revenue; they measure different things and are not mixed anywhere above.
HPCL carries both quarter-on-quarter and year-on-year bases for the same reason.
Markets are watchlist-only.
Nothing here is a tip, a target or a buy/sell call.
Edition 18.
The long read: "Seven years for the promise" - Jio's road from the 2019 AGM stage to today's closing bell on India's largest IPO.
On 12 August 2019, Mukesh Ambani stood before shareholders at Reliance Industries' 42nd annual general meeting in Mumbai and made two promises in one speech.

The first was about debt: Reliance, which had invested nearly ₹3.5 lakh crore in Jio's digital infrastructure by then and carried net debt of ₹1,54,478 crore, would become a zero-net-debt company within eighteen months.

The second was about the stock market: "We will induct leading global partners in Jio and Reliance Retail in the next few quarters, and move towards the listing of both these companies within the next five years" (full text of the speech, Business Today; firstpost's AGM report).
The arithmetic he was offering was seductive.
Jio had upended Indian telecom in three years - free voice, data priced at a fraction of the incumbents', and a subscriber base that had blown past 300 million.
The oil-and-petrochemicals cash cow that funded it was mature.
If the old business paid down the debt and the new businesses listed, shareholders would own the future outright and unencumbered.
Both halves of the plan had dates on them.
Both dates would slip - one by a little, one by a lot.
What happened next, in the middle of a global lockdown, has no real parallel in Indian corporate history.
Between late April and late June 2020, a procession of the world's largest investors bought into Jio Platforms - the holding company for the telecom and digital businesses.

On 22 April, Facebook paid $5.7 billion (about ₹43,574 crore) for roughly 9.99% - the anchor transaction of the whole exercise, struck while the world's airports were shut, and the deal that set the price everyone else paid around: an implied valuation of about ₹4.36 lakh crore for Jio Platforms (computed from the disclosed stake and price).
Silver Lake, Vista, KKR, General Atlantic, Mubadala, ADIA, TPG and others followed.

On 19 June 2020, Reliance issued a press release whose headline did the counting itself: "Reliance raises over ₹168,818 crore in just 58 days" - ₹115,693.95 crore of it from Jio's new investors, the rest from a rights issue.
"I have fulfilled my promise to the shareholders by making Reliance net debt-free much before our original schedule of 31st March 2021." - Mukesh Ambani, Reliance press release, 19 June 2020.
Net debt had stood at ₹1,61,035 crore on 31 March 2020.
On 15 July, at the 2020 AGM, Google closed the round: $4.5 billion (₹33,737 crore) for 7.7% and a board seat (Reuters).

In all, roughly a third of Jio Platforms - about 33% - was sold for about ₹1.52 lakh crore (~$20 billion) in one pandemic year, and Ambani told shareholders the group was ending "our current cycle of capital raising" (Reuters, 16 July 2020).
The listing half of the 2019 promise looked close behind: Bloomberg reported in May 2020 that bankers were preparing Jio for an overseas IPO within 12 to 24 months.
Five years, it turned out, was going to be comfortable.
The first crack appeared in the old business, not the new one.
The August 2019 speech had also announced a non-binding deal to sell 20% of Reliance's oil-to-chemicals arm to Saudi Aramco for $15 billion - the final leg of the deleveraging plan.
On 25 November 2021, after two years of valuation differences, the companies called it off (Reuters).
Reliance said it would re-evaluate; the O2C stake sale never came back in that form.
The second crack was a phone.
In late 2021, Jio and Google launched the JioPhone Next - a ₹6,500 smartphone meant to convert India's remaining 2G users into Jio customers, the hardware expression of the Google partnership.
It flopped.

Within six months the price had been cut about 40%; media reports put sales around two million units against ambitions near 50 million; inventory was liquidated, and Jio retreated to selling own-brand 5G phones instead (The Ken's reconstruction, April 2023).
The lesson Jio drew was expensive and useful: distribution and price were never the bottleneck - the product was.
And the listing?
The five-year mark - August 2024 - came and went with no prospectus.
By the 2023 AGM, the Economic Times was running pieces explaining why the "RJio IPO dream shown by Ambani 5 years back won't come true soon".
Reliance Retail, the other company named in the promise, remains unlisted to this day.
The promise had not died; it had just quietly gone overdue, the way large promises do when nobody is forced to mention them.
While the listing slipped, the business compounded.

Jio's own annual report for FY 2025-26 - read for this story, not via summaries - records revenue from operations of ₹1,46,885 crore, up 14.6% on the year; EBITDA of ₹76,255 crore, up 18.8%, at a 51.9% margin; 524.4 million subscribers as of March 2026, each consuming an average of 42.3 GB of data and 988 voice minutes a month (Jio Platforms annual report, investor relations).
Profit after tax for FY26 was ₹30,049 crore, per RHP figures cited in IPO notes.
The growth engine changed character over the seven years, and this is the part the 2019 audience could not have foreseen.
Subscriber growth is no longer the story - India is connected.
Pricing is.

Industry-wide tariff hikes, led by Jio, have taken average revenue per user from ₹181.7 a month before the July 2024 hike to ₹206.2 after it and ₹215.6 in the June 2026 quarter (RHP figures as cited in IPO notes).

The second engine is the home: fixed broadband connections grew from 11.2 million in March 2024 to 28.6 million by June 2026, and rental income from the set-top boxes and routers in those homes more than doubled to ₹3,907 crore in FY26 (RHP figures via IPO notes).
Jio also built the country's only standalone 5G network - the architecture that does not lean on a 4G core.
On 14 October 2026, Reliance announced that Jio Platforms had filed its red herring prospectus with SEBI (ril.com corporate announcements).
The issue: 27 crore fresh shares at ₹1,065 to ₹1,119, raising ₹30,213 crore at the cap - the largest IPO India has seen, passing Hyundai Motor India's ₹27,858.75 crore (Fortune India).

At the cap, the market is being asked to pay about ₹10.3 lakh crore - roughly $108 billion - which would make Jio Platforms India's fourth-most-valuable listed company on debut, behind only its own parent, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank (Times of India).
It would also tip the RIL group's combined market value past the Tata group's.
Read the structure and you can see what the company wants the money to say.
It is 100% fresh equity - not one of the 2020 investors is selling a share.
Meta (through Jaadhu Holdings), Google, PIF, KKR, Vista, Silver Lake, Mubadala, General Atlantic, ADIA, TPG - all of them stay in at the IPO price.

The proceeds have a deliberately unglamorous job: prepaying three external commercial borrowings - dollar and yen loans due March to June 2028, carrying 1.40% to 5.13% - about ₹27,500 crore of it in FY27, with general corporate purposes capped at a quarter of the raise (RHP figures via IPO note).
This is not a cash-out; it is a balance-sheet swap, equity for debt, taken at a price the 2020 investors are happy to hold.
Which brings back the anchor transaction.
Facebook's April 2020 cheque - ₹43,574 crore for 9.99% - implied a valuation of about ₹4.36 lakh crore (computed).

The ₹10.3 lakh crore cap price is about 2.4 times that, in rupees, over six and a half years (computed) - a respectable, not spectacular, return for waiting, and exactly the kind of number a prospectus does not print.
The sellers of 2020 became the holders of 2026: that, more than any grey-market premium, is the informed-money verdict on the price.
Three things, honestly counted.
The timeline: "within the next five years" became seven, and one of the two companies named in the promise - Reliance Retail - is still unlisted.
The phone: the JioPhone Next was a misread of what would move 2G users, and it died in about a year.
And the Aramco deal: the elegant 2019 plan to deleverage partly through the old business ended with the new business doing all the work.
None of these is fatal; together they explain why this listing arrives in 2026 priced on pricing power rather than in 2021 priced on subscriber growth.
Which leaves today.
Bidding closes at 5 PM, UPI mandates at 7 PM.

The settled print after day two: 5.57 times subscribed on BSE data - institutions at 13.29 times their allocation, retail at 1.54 times, having crossed full coverage only on day two (BSE consolidated data as of 7 PM Thursday, via NDTV Profit's timestamped record).
Allotment is expected Monday.
The bell, if the schedule holds, is Wednesday 28 October.
Seven years ago the promise was made from a stage in Mumbai to a hall of shareholders who had lent the company ₹1.5 lakh crore of patience.
This morning the grey market - unofficial, unregulated - prices the debut at about 22% above the cap.
The 2020 investors, offered the exit, declined it.

The question Wednesday answers is whether the public market pays ₹10.3 lakh crore for what seven years actually built: not the company that adds the most subscribers, but the one that decides what India pays to be connected.

This story's working thesis is that the seven-year wait converted a telecom operator into India's consumer-infrastructure layer, and that ₹10.3 lakh crore is a fair price for the pricing power that comes with it.
Three things would cut it down.
First, the listing itself: a debut that breaks the ₹1,119 cap and stays below it is the market rejecting the price outright.

Second, the ARPU engine: the FY24-26 revenue growth - about 15.8% a year, per RHP figures via notes - rests on tariff hikes, and hikes have a political ceiling; a stalled ARPU with 5G returns still building would squeeze the story from both sides.
Third, the home: if broadband additions flatten before the set-top-box economics mature, the second engine arrives too late to matter.
Watch the first on Wednesday, the second every quarter.
